title: Class 4 Maths Syllabus: A Parent’s Complete Guide + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 4 Maths Syllabus: Parent’s Guide + Quiz
meta_desc: The full class 4 maths syllabus explained strand by strand — what mastery looks like, warning signs to watch, plus a free 8-question quiz for parents.
excerpt: Class 4 is the year maths gets wider, not just harder. Here is the whole NCERT-aligned syllabus, strand by strand — what your child should master, and the one warning sign to watch in each.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
When my niece moved into Class 4, the maths did not just get harder — it got wider. Suddenly there were lakhs, long division, fractions, decimals, area, angles and the 24-hour clock, all in one year. Most parents I speak to in Tier-2 cities feel the same jolt. So this is the map I wish I had handed them: the whole class 4 maths syllabus, strand by strand, with what ‘mastery’ actually looks like and the one warning sign to watch in each. It is NCERT and CBSE aligned, and deliberately broad rather than deep — each strand has its own method worth a separate lesson.

Think of Class 4 as the bridge from primary counting to real arithmetic. Nothing here is optional; the topics stack on each other. A wobble in place value shows up three chapters later in division.

Numbers, place value and the four operations

Place value to lakhs. Numbers jump from thousands into lakhs. Mastery is reading, writing and comparing 5- and 6-digit numbers — and knowing that in 4,53,210 the 5 means fifty thousand. Warning sign: a child who reads the number aloud but freezes when asked which digit sits in the thousands place.

Rounding and estimation. Rounding to the nearest ten, hundred and thousand turns messy numbers into quick estimates. Mastery is rounding 4,678 to 4,700 and using it to sense-check an answer. Warning sign: rounding correctly but shrugging when the estimate and the exact answer sit miles apart.

Adding and subtracting large numbers. Addition and subtraction now run to four and five digits with carrying and borrowing across zeros. Mastery is a clean, aligned column method. Warning sign: mistakes that cluster around borrowing from a zero, as in 5,002 − 1,847.

Multi-digit multiplication. Multiplication moves to two-digit by two-digit and three-digit by one-digit. Mastery means secure tables to 10 and a confident column method. Warning sign: the method is right but the tables underneath are slow — that is the real gap, not the layout.

Long division with remainders. This is the year’s steepest climb. Mastery is dividing a three-digit number by a single digit and reading the remainder inside a word problem. Warning sign: a child who lands the quotient but ignores what the remainder actually means.

Factors and multiples. Here the language of number relationships begins. Mastery is listing the factors of 24 or the multiples of 6 and spotting common ones. Warning sign: muddling the two — factors divide into a number, multiples count up from it.

Number patterns. Patterns and simple rules stretch early algebraic thinking. Mastery is continuing a sequence and stating its rule, such as ‘add 7’ or ‘double it’. Warning sign: extending a pattern by copying the look of it without being able to say why.

Fractions, decimals and money

Equivalent fractions and operations. Fractions grow from naming parts to equivalence and same-denominator addition. Mastery is seeing that 2/4 and 1/2 are the same, and adding 1/5 + 2/5 correctly. Warning sign: adding the denominators too, so 1/5 + 2/5 becomes 3/10.

Decimals (tenths and hundredths). Decimals arrive as tenths and hundredths, tied to money and measurement. Mastery is reading 0.7 and 0.25 and placing them on a number line. Warning sign: believing 0.7 is smaller than 0.25 because 25 looks like the bigger number.

Money. Money problems fold rupees and paise into all four operations. Mastery is making bills, giving change and converting ₹3.50 into 350 paise. Warning sign: correct arithmetic but a decimal point slipped one place in the total.

Measurement, geometry and data handling

Measurement conversions. Length, weight and capacity come with metric conversions. Mastery is converting 2 km to 2,000 m or 1,500 g to 1.5 kg. Warning sign: multiplying when they should divide between units, or the reverse.

Area and perimeter. These two ideas split ‘distance around’ from ‘space inside’. Mastery is counting squares for area, adding sides for perimeter, and keeping the units straight. Warning sign: one method used for both, or dropping the square from cm².

Time and the 24-hour clock. Time work extends to the 24-hour clock, elapsed time and calendars. Mastery is reading 15:40 as 3:40 pm and working out how long a journey took. Warning sign: getting stuck the moment the time crosses an hour, like 10:50 to 11:20.

2D shapes and symmetry. Geometry revisits 2D shapes and lines of symmetry. Mastery is naming shapes by their sides and drawing a line of symmetry on a rectangle or a letter. Warning sign: assuming every shape has exactly one line of symmetry.

Angles. Angles appear as amounts of turn, with the right angle as the anchor. Mastery is spotting angles smaller or larger than a right angle. Warning sign: judging an angle by how long its arms are drawn rather than by the opening between them.

Line plots and data. Data handling uses tally marks, pictographs and simple line plots. Mastery is reading a chart and answering ‘how many more’ questions. Warning sign: reading a single bar or symbol correctly but stumbling on the comparison.

The class 4 maths syllabus at a glance

StrandWhat mastery looks like
Place value to lakhsRead, write and compare 6-digit numbers
Large-number add & subtractCarry and borrow across zeros cleanly
Multiplication & division2-digit × 2-digit; divide with remainders
Factors & multiplesList and compare them without mixing up
FractionsRecognise equivalents; add same denominators
Decimals & moneyTenths, hundredths and ₹ with paise
MeasurementConvert km–m, kg–g, l–ml
Area, perimeter & anglesSeparate the ideas; use a right angle to compare
Time & data24-hour clock; read plots and charts

How to use this map at home

You do not teach 16 strands at once. Follow the school’s order, and let the earlier number work stay strong before the later topics lean on it. A simple rhythm that works:

  • Fix place value and tables first — almost everything else rests on them.
  • Treat long division as a term-long project, not a one-week topic.
  • Keep fractions and decimals concrete with paper strips and rupee coins.
  • Do a little mixed revision each weekend so the child chooses the method, not you.

One honest caveat: breadth is the trap of Class 4. It is tempting to race through the list, but a child who half-knows ten strands is weaker than one who truly owns six. Depth first, coverage second.

quiz.title: Class 4 Maths Syllabus Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions sampling the whole Class 4 year — place value, operations, fractions, decimals, measurement and geometry. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: In the number 4,53,210, what does the digit 5 stand for?
questions.explanation: Counting from the right, the 5 sits in the ten-thousands place, so it means fifty thousand.

questions.q: What is 4,678 rounded to the nearest hundred?
questions.explanation: The tens digit is 7, which is 5 or more, so round up: 4,678 becomes 4,700.
5 × 69 = 345, and 348 − 345 = 3, so the answer is 69 remainder 3.
2/4 simplifies to 1/2, so they represent the same amount.
0.7 means seven tenths, which is more than 0.5, 0.25 or 0.09. More digits does not mean a bigger number.

questions.q: How many metres are there in 2 kilometres?
A square has a side of 6 cm. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: Perimeter is the distance around: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 cm. (36 cm² would be the area.)

questions.q: What time is 15:40 on a 12-hour clock?
questions.explanation: Subtract 12 from 15 to get 3, and it is afternoon, so 15:40 is 3:40 pm.

faq.q: What are the main topics in the Class 4 maths syllabus?
faq.a: The NCERT-aligned Class 4 year covers place value to lakhs, rounding, the four operations on large numbers, factors and multiples, fractions, decimals, money, measurement conversions, area and perimeter, time and the 24-hour clock, 2D shapes and symmetry, angles, and simple data handling.

faq.q: Which Class 4 topic do children struggle with most?
faq.a: Long division with remainders, usually. It combines tables, subtraction and place value all at once, so any weakness underneath surfaces here. Treat it as a term-long project rather than a single chapter.

faq.q: Is the Class 4 maths syllabus the same for CBSE and state boards?
faq.a: The core strands are broadly the same because most boards follow the NCERT framework. The order of chapters and the depth of word problems can differ, so check your child’s own textbook for sequence.

faq.q: How can I tell if my child is on track in Class 4?
faq.a: Look for understanding, not just correct answers. A child on track can explain why 2/4 equals 1/2 or what a remainder means, not only compute it. Slow, shaky tables are the most common early warning sign.
